# 1.3 - Quartiles, IQR, and Box Plots {.unnumbered}

The median cuts data into two halves. What if you cut each half in half again?

You get four parts. Each part has about 25% of the data. The numbers that make those cuts are called {{< glink slug="quartile" text="quartiles" >}}.

In this lesson, you find quartiles, use them to measure spread, and draw a {{< glink "box plot" >}}.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I find Q1, the median, and Q3.
- [ ] I find the five-number summary and the IQR.
- [ ] I make a box plot.
:::

{{< learn >}}

### 1.3.1 - Finding Quartiles

:::{.remember title="How to Find the Quartiles"}
1. Put the data in order.
2. Find the **median**. It splits the data into a **lower half** and an **upper half**.
3. **Q1** = the median of the lower half.
4. **Q3** = the median of the upper half.

**Odd number of values?** Leave the median out of both halves.
:::

**Example 1:** an odd number of values (11)

3, 4, 6, 7, 9, **10**, 12, 13, 15, 18, 20

The median is **10**. Leave it out of the halves.

| Lower half | Upper half |
|:---:|:---:|
| 3, 4, **6**, 7, 9 | 12, 13, **15**, 18, 20 |
| Q1 = 6 | Q3 = 15 |

**Example 2:** an even number of values (10)

1, 3, 4, 6, **7**, **9**, 10, 12, 14, 18

There are two middle values, 7 and 9. The median is $(7 + 9) \div 2 = 8$.

| Lower half | Upper half |
|:---:|:---:|
| 1, 3, **4**, 6, 7 | 9, 10, **12**, 14, 18 |
| Q1 = 4 | Q3 = 12 |

***

### 1.3.2 - The Five-Number Summary and the IQR

The {{< glink "five-number summary" >}} is five numbers:

**minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum**

The {{< glink "interquartile range" >}} (IQR) shows how spread out the **middle half** of the data is.

$$
\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1
$$

For Example 1: IQR $= 15 - 6 = 9$.

For Example 2: IQR $= 12 - 4 = 8$.

:::{.you-try-m title="Find the five-number summary and the IQR."}
5, 9, 2, 7, 4, 8, 3
:::
:::{.answer title="Answer"}
In order: 2, 3, 4, **5**, 7, 8, 9. The median is 5.

Lower half: 2, **3**, 4. So Q1 = 3.

Upper half: 7, **8**, 9. So Q3 = 8.

Five-number summary: 2, 3, 5, 8, 9. IQR $= 8 - 3 = 5$.
:::

***

### 1.3.3 - Box Plots

A {{< glink "box plot" >}} draws the five-number summary on a number line. Here is Example 1.

![](/images/Unit_1/1.3_box_plot_example.svg){width="640px" fig-align="center"}

- The **box** goes from Q1 to Q3. Its length is the IQR.
- The **line inside the box** is the median.
- The **whiskers** go out to the minimum and the maximum.

:::{.gotcha title="Same count, not same width"}
The 4 parts have the same **number of values**, not the same width. A short part means the values are packed close together. A long part means they are spread out.
:::

:::{.think title="Why use the IQR instead of the range?"}
The range is maximum minus minimum. One extreme value changes it a lot.

The IQR only uses the middle half of the data. One extreme value does not move it. This is like the median and the mean.
:::

**Five-Number Summary**

1. Find the five-number summary and the IQR.

   4, 8, 1, 6, 9, 3, 7

2. Find the five-number summary and the IQR.

   12, 15, 10, 20, 18, 11, 16, 14

***

**Box Plots**

3. Eleven students recorded how many minutes they spent on homework last night.

   30, 10, 45, 5, 25, 60, 15, 30, 10, 40, 20

   a. Find the five-number summary.

   b. Make a box plot.

   c. What is the IQR? What does it tell you?

4. Twelve students counted how many texts they sent in one hour.

   13, 2, 20, 8, 30, 12, 5, 18, 10, 24, 8, 15

   a. Find the five-number summary.

   b. Make a box plot.

   c. Which part of the box plot is the longest? What does that tell you about the data?
